opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think about it pretty practically, almost selfishly. I start from: what are the chores in my own house that I actually hate doing, and that happen often enough that a robot doing them would change my week? Laundry folding, loading and unloading the dishwasher, picking up clutter off the floor, tidying the kitchen counters. Those are the things that eat time every single day.

The trap a lot of people fall into is building a robot that's impressive in a demo but not useful at home. A demo is one task, one setup, good lighting, someone resetting the scene. A home is the opposite. Every house is different, things move around, kids leave toys everywhere, the lighting changes, and the robot has to recover from its own mistakes without someone babysitting it. So for me "useful" means it works reliably enough, across enough of the mess of real life, that I trust it to run while I'm not watching. If I have to supervise it, I might as well do the chore myself.

That pushes you toward a few design choices. First, the hardware should be cheap and robust rather than exotic. You want something you can afford to have in a home, that won't hurt anyone, and that you can fix when it breaks. You don't need a perfect humanoid. A mobile base with a decent arm and a good gripper covers a surprising amount of household work.

Second, the intelligence has to come from learning, not hand-engineering every task. You can't write a program for every possible kitchen. So you want a system that learns from lots of demonstrations and data, generalizes to new objects and layouts, and gets better the more it's used. That's very much the lesson we learned from deep learning in vision and language: scale the data, make the tooling easy, let the community iterate fast.

And third, and this is the part I care about coming from the PyTorch side, the whole thing should be open and hackable. If the hardware designs, the software stack, and the datasets are open, then thousands of people can build these, try them in their own homes, and contribute back. That diversity of homes is exactly the data you need. I think that's how you actually get to a robot that's useful in a household: not one company perfecting it in a lab, but lots of people iterating on it in real kitchens.

r001.rationale: The response discusses household chores and the gap between demos and real homes, but does not identify work with physical robots as a productivity bottleneck in robotics development.

r002.rationale: It recommends cheap, robust hardware and learning from data, but does not say machine learning should compensate for hardware imprecision.

r003.rationale: It does not describe verbal interaction with the robot or the robot asking clarification questions.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is, the first thing you have to do is be honest about what "useful" means. When people imagine a household robot, they picture something like a humanoid that walks in and does everything a person does. And I think that framing is actually what makes the problem feel impossible. Because then you're signing up for general intelligence, dexterous manipulation, safety around kids and pets, all at once.

So I start from the other direction. I look at my own house and I ask, what are the tasks that are annoying, repetitive, and bounded? Loading and unloading the dishwasher. Folding laundry. Picking stuff up off the floor. Those are things where, if you got even a mediocre version working, people would actually pay for it, and more importantly they'd tolerate failures. A robot that folds 80 percent of your laundry and leaves a pile of weird shirts is still a net win. A robot that can't be trusted around your toddler is a product nobody ships.

The second thing is that the hardware has gotten way less of a bottleneck than people assume. Cheap arms, decent cameras, the actuators are fine. The real gap is in the learning stack. We don't have good ways to collect data at scale in homes, because every home is different, the lighting is different, the objects are different. So a lot of my thinking is really about the data flywheel. How do you get a robot into homes early enough, doing something simple enough, that it's gathering the experience you need to make it good at the next thing?

And honestly that's the lesson from everything else in deep learning. You don't get there by designing the perfect system up front. You get there by putting something imperfect in the world, with really good tooling around it so you can iterate fast, and letting the data and the feedback loop pull you forward. The robot in my house is going to look kind of dumb at first. That's fine. The question is whether it gets smarter every month.

r001.rationale: The response says hardware is less of a bottleneck and identifies the learning stack and home data collection as the main gaps; it does not identify physical robot work as a development productivity bottleneck.

r002.rationale: It mentions cheap arms and says actuators are adequate, but does not propose using machine learning to compensate for hardware imprecision to lower costs.

r003.rationale: It discusses bounded household chores but does not propose verbal guidance or clarification questions.

astra-6.text:
I would start with the task, rather than the robot. What is something in my house that I would actually want help with? Laundry is a good example. But even “do the laundry” is a whole collection of problems: finding the clothes, picking them up, loading the machine, getting them out, folding them, putting them away.

So I’d pick a small part of that and ask whether we can make it reliable. If I have to stand next to the robot and rescue it every few minutes, it hasn’t really saved me any work. A demo where it folds one shirt is exciting, but the useful thing is being able to leave it with a pile of clothes and go do something else.

That also changes how you think about intelligence. It doesn’t necessarily need to understand everything about my household. It needs enough understanding to do its job, recognize when something has gone wrong, and ask for help. I think that’s a much more concrete place to start than saying, let’s build a general-purpose robot and then figure out what it can do.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses whether a household robot can reliably complete chores, but does not identify physical robot work as a productivity bottleneck in robotics development.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss lowering hardware costs or using machine learning to compensate for imprecise hardware.

r003.rationale: The robot may recognize problems and ask for help, but the candidate does not propose guiding it through chores via verbal interaction or clarification questions.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d start with a task I actually want done, like clearing the dinner table. It sounds simple, but there’s a lot hidden in it. The robot has to recognize what belongs where, pick up a glass without breaking it, deal with a plate that still has food on it, and figure out what to do when something goes wrong.

For me, the interesting question is how much teaching that takes. Can I show it a few times and then have it generalize to different dishes, a different arrangement, or somebody leaving a bag on the floor? If I have to engineer my entire house around the robot, that’s a pretty big cost.

So I’d want something with a fairly narrow initial job, but the ability to learn from corrections. And it needs to know when to stop and ask for help. A robot that reliably does one chore and occasionally asks me a question would already be useful.

r002.rationale: It mentions adapting to varied situations, but does not propose using machine learning to compensate for hardware imprecision or reduce hardware costs.

r003.rationale: It says the robot should ask for help, but does not describe guiding chores through verbal interaction or clarification questions.
